chapter_theme: The sacred temple (திருக்கோயில்): moving a fixed lingam, taking a stone from a temple wall, letting its rites lapse or having them done by an unfit priest brings ruin on the king and the land: disease, failed rain, theft and famine. Each verse ends on Nandi's word or command.
structure_note: Two verses on damage to the temple's fabric (515, 516), two on lapsed worship (517, 518) and one on an unfit priest (519).

515.reading: If one pulls up a fixed lingam and sets it up elsewhere, the kingdom loses its stability before the deed is done, and great disease befalls him before he dies; so Nandi the guardian declared.
515.nuance: தாவர லிங்கம் is the installed, immovable lingam, as against a movable one. The verse does not say whose disease is meant; it is usually taken as the one who moves it, while the king's realm suffers too.

516.reading: If one takes away even a single stone from the wall of a temple someone built, the command of the Lord of heaven will have even an anointed king cut down, and will have him cut down even if he is a sage or a Vedic Brahmin.
516.nuance: The verse spares no rank: anointed kings, sages and Brahmins alike. முட்டுவிக்கும் may mean 'brings to an end' or 'obstructs'.

517.reading: If the pujas ordained in all the temples of the one who kicked Death lapse, unbearable disease grows, the earth has no rain, and even praiseworthy kings lose their strength in war.
517.nuance: கூற்றுதைத்தான் recalls Siva kicking Death to save Markandeya. The verse makes worship a cause of rain, not merely dependent on it.

518.reading: If the pujas in the temple of the First One stop, harm comes to kings, the bounty of the rains declines, and housebreaking and theft increase in the land; so our rare Nandi declared.
518.nuance: The text reads வாரி (abundance, or the sea); the variant மாரி makes it the rains. கன்னம் is housebreaking, from the hole made in the wall.

519.reading: If a Brahmin who has only the name worships the Lord, it becomes a vile disease for warring kings and famine for the land; so glorious Nandi declared after due thought.
519.nuance: பேர்கொண்ட பார்ப்பான் can mean a Brahmin in name only, or a Brahmin of renown. Tradition takes it of one not qualified or initiated for temple worship, but the verse does not say what he lacks.

links.note: The same link between rain and worship, run in opposite directions: in the Kural, if the sky dries up, festival and worship cease even for the gods; in Tirumular, if the pujas lapse, the earth has no rain.

Both list what declines when a guardian fails: in the Kural, if the king does not guard, cows give less and Brahmins forget their books; in Tirumular, if the temple pujas stop, kings come to harm and theft grows. The king is the cause in one and the casualty in the other.
241 says that when those whose ignorance remains take up the tuft and thread, the land withers and the king loses standing; 519 says the same of a Brahmin in name only who worships in the temple.

Kural 559 says that if the king bends justice ('முறைகோடி'), the sky withholds its rain. Tirumanthiram 517 says that if the pujas in the temples of the one who kicked Death lapse, the earth has no rain ('அவனி மழையின்றி') and kings lose their strength. The same pattern, a failure at the centre followed by drought, appears in two domains: the Kural places it in the king's justice, the Tirumanthiram in the temple's worship, and makes the king suffer it too.
